summary: Abhay Bhushan's reply to Bob Braden's comments on FTP in RFC 430. He agrees that most should go into the forthcoming official specification, and answers them one by one, in preparation for the March 16 FTP meeting at BBN. It is a discussion paper.

plainLanguage.summary: One person answers a list of complaints about the file-sending rules, saying which ones he agrees with.

subtitle: A discussion of FTP protocol refinements and technical feedback

tldr.problem: Bob Braden had submitted detailed comments on RFC 430 proposing FTP improvements; several issues needed discussion before finalizing the official FTP specification.
tldr.mechanism: Abhay Bhushan reviewed Braden's comments point by point, agreeing with most and offering technical responses, and raised additional suggestions for the forthcoming FTP meeting.
tldr.outcome: This discussion fed into the March 1973 FTP meeting at BBN, helping shape the direction of the evolving file transfer protocol.

today: RFC 463 is a historical discussion that contributed to the evolution of FTP. The final FTP specification, RFC 959, ultimately standardized many of the protocol aspects discussed here.

sections.title: Response to Protocol Comments
sections.content: Abhay Bhushan of MIT-DMCG responded to Bob Braden's detailed comments on RFC 430, which had proposed several improvements to the File Transfer Protocol. Bhushan acknowledged that most of Braden's suggestions were useful and should be incorporated into the forthcoming official FTP specification. This response, combined with the results of an earlier FTP subgroup meeting at BBN on January 25, would inform the March 16 FTP meeting.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone sent in a list of ways to improve the file-sending rules, and Bhushan said which ones he agreed with.

sections.title: Command Sequencing and Data Encoding
sections.content: Key improvements Bhushan supported included using bit flag coding for descriptors rather than other methods, and tightening the command-reply sequence so programs could reliably automate FTP operations. He suggested that a required 300-reply greeting upon connection would eliminate the need for programs to wait an arbitrary time before issuing commands. He also proposed allowing multiple parameter changes in a single command line to improve efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: When sending a file, the computer talking to the server needs clear rules about what to send and when, so programs can do it without getting stuck.

sections.title: Mail and Password Handling
sections.content: Bhushan noted that while some hosts might not allow password changes via FTP (as on Multics), a standard format could still be defined for those that do. For network mail, he raised issues about accepting mail to multiple users, standardizing user name formats (using NIC idents or last names), and establishing uniform conventions for tagging mail with sender, date, and time. He suggested that bulk mail might be stored in a user directory with a notification message rather than dumped on the user's console.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail sent over the network needed rules for who it was from, when it arrived, and how to handle a lot of mail without overwhelming someone.

references.text: Braden, R., "Comments on RFC 430", RFC 430, February 1973.
Bhushan, A., "Revised FTP reply codes", RFC 454, February 1973.
